entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Lighthouse of Alexandria, constructed around 280 BCE on the small island of Pharos in Egypt, stands as one of the most iconic symbols of ancient engineering and maritime navigation. Designed by the architect Sostratus of Cnidus under the reign of Ptolemy II, this towering structure not only served as a beacon for sailors navigating the treacherous waters of the Mediterranean but also represented the wealth and cultural prowess of Hellenistic Alexandria. Its height, estimated at over 100 meters, made it one of the tallest man-made structures of the ancient world, and its light source, believed to be a combination of an open flame and polished bronze mirrors, was a marvel of technological ingenuity.

The Lighthouse was not merely a navigational aid; it was a statement of power and sophistication, reflecting the ambitions of the Ptolemaic dynasty to establish Alexandria as a center of commerce and culture. The beacon's construction took approximately twelve years and was completed in 280 BCE, during a period when Alexandria was the most prominent city in the Mediterranean. Over the centuries, it withstood numerous earthquakes, although it ultimately succumbed to a series of destructive quakes in the 14th century CE, which led to its collapse and the eventual loss of its architectural grandeur.

The legacy of the Lighthouse of Alexandria is profound, influencing architectural design and maritime navigation for centuries. Its design inspired the construction of numerous lighthouses throughout history, including the famous Tower of Hercules in Spain. Moreover, it serves as a symbol of the ancient world's technological achievements and has been immortalized in literature, art, and popular culture, influencing how subsequent civilizations viewed progress and innovation. The phrase 'Pharos' itself became synonymous with lighthouses, underscoring its enduring influence.
